newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela to send Colombian drug kingpin to U.S..
newsitem.headline: Venezuela to send Colombian drug kingpin to U.S..

text.p: Venezuela's Supreme Court ruled on Thursday that suspected Colombian drug kingpin Justo Pastor Perafan should be extradited to the United States to face drug trafficking charges.
Venezuela's Foreign Minister, Miguel Angel Burelli Rivas, said it would probably take a couple of days to process the necessary documentation for the extradition.
Perafan, 50, who was using an alias and had undergone plastic surgery and hair implants to change his appearance, was said to be one of the wealthiest Colombian cocaine lords still on the run.
Believed to possess a personal fortune of $12 billion, Perafan was the last Colombian drug lord not in jail or dead. He was to be handed over to a New York state court.
He is wanted in New York on drug trafficking and possession charges, Supreme Court vice-President Ismael Rodriguez Salazar said.
Perafan was carrying false papers when he was captured in April by Venezuelan police in the western town of San Cristobal, across the border from Colombia, police sources said.
"This is a very positive sign and sends a message to drug traffickers throughout the world that Venezuelan justice works efficiently in these cases," U.S. Ambassador John Maisto told reporters.
"(The decision) underlines that the fight against (drug) traffickers is one which cuts across borders," Maisto added.
Perafan, a former baker of humble origins, had asked to be sent back to Colombia, which had also lodged an extradition request with Venezuela.
But many legal experts and Colombia's police chief, Gen. Rosso Jose Serrano, said he would face a tougher sentence in the United States.

Colombian officials said they would not challenge Venezuela's decision. "We respect and comply with the decision which has been taken regarding this case," Colombia's Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia said in Bogota.
The decision to extradite Perafan came as Colombia's Senate started debating a bill to restore extradition treaties with the United States for drug traffickers.
Colombia suspended extraditions in 1991 under pressure from a wave of violence by drug cartels opposed to the measure.
